column1: # THE MAP THE PARTY HAS. Append-only; current knowledge is DERIVED.
# *** THE TRUE MAP IS campaign/places.tsv AND IT IS EXACT. THIS IS WHAT THEY
# *** KNOW ABOUT IT, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT THING AND CHANGES.
# The campaign already draws this distinction one level down: `mapdb` separates
# what a square IS from `cells.seen`, what the party has actually looked at, and
# `campaign/journal.md` is explicitly "what the party thinks it knows, as
# distinct from cells.seen". This is that, above ground.
# level:
#   known    been there and attended. They could put it on a map and be right
#   vague    *** they know roughly where it is and would not bet on it. ***
#            Either hearsay with a direction, or somewhere they PASSED THROUGH
#            IN A HURRY -- technically been, practically not. `precision_ft` is
#            the radius they would actually stand behind
#   heard    named, no position. Wraye is "three days east of Ludbury and it has
#            a library" and THAT IS ALL THEY HAVE
#   unknown  not in their world yet. The default; a place with no row is unknown
# A LOG and not a table, because knowledge is ACQUIRED ON A DAY BY AN EVENT --
# the same reasoning that made loops.tsv a log. `known` versus `vague` is a
# judgment and cannot be derived, so it is logged; but `overland.py check` will
# flag any place the party demonstrably spent a day at with no row here, which
# catches the DM forgetting.
# *** AND THIS IS A SPOILER SURFACE. *** `overland.py` renders the PARTY'S map by
# default and needs --true for the other one. If they have never been to Wraye,
# their map must not have a dot at its exact coordinates. CHECKLIST section 8.

Home since day 1. Market, the square, Wend's barn, the inn
They came IN by the Draycot road before expedition 1 -- so they have walked it -- but they arrived as strangers with no reason to survey it, and did not see the hall until day 14
The north road, walked repeatedly from day 6
Six days of patrolling its whole day's-walk circuit
The first ride down, day 13-14. Seen properly, gate and all
Dave and Sim rode out; two years of fleece in a stone barn
Coll's crew graded the trail and built it
Eight expeditions in and out

*** THE THIRD CASE, EXACTLY. *** They have been INSIDE more than anyone, and mapdb holds level 1 to ten feet -- but where the hill SITS relative to the road is still "about an hour off the turning, up the outcrop". Nobody has surveyed the outside
The wool caravan, days 25-27. Gate duty, the market, the rosewood
90 gp for a barn, seed and a winter, paid at his gate
Eight miles cross-country and back; they have walked it twice
THREE DAYS EAST OF LUDBURY AND IT HAS A LIBRARY. That is the whole of it, and it is the only lead on the ring
Three days down, market day, Trebb's yard, the church, Ossery's shutters
Dave rode over from the road and paid 31 gp at his door
Nan named it: a widow with three years of wool in a loft who would take a fair price off anybody who asked her properly. NOBODY HAS BEEN
Nan named it: two holdings past it roll their wool wet. NOBODY HAS BEEN

*** THE ROUTE, AND THEY COULD NOT DRAW IT. *** Wat rode down and turned off; Dave rode over from the road on day 62. Both of them found it by asking or by being told, and NOBODY HAS EVER SAID WHICH MILESTONE IT IS. They know Lyde is a day off the southern road, west. They do not know where the turning is to five miles
Four miles of track east off the north road, taken by cart twice. This one they could point at

*** UPGRADED FROM `heard` 2026-09-12. *** They know it EXISTS, that it is reachable by road out of Ludbury, and that it is three days east -- so they could put a finger on a region, which is more than nothing and less than a position. The radius is thirty miles because "east" is one of eight compass points and a 45-degree wedge at seventy-five miles is that wide. *** The record says three days east of LUDBURY, not Marchford -- calendar.md:103, the distance table. ***

*** CORRECTED SAME DAY. *** The row above made this vague on the reasoning that nobody had surveyed which milestone it is. The player caught it: DAVE RODE TO LYDE AND BACK on day 62 and Wat before him. A man who has ridden to a place and home again knows where he turned off. It is KNOWN
They WALKED IN by it before expedition 1 and have not been back. They know the Draycot road runs on south-west and roughly how far they came; they could not draw it

column1: # ---- THE WAYS. Every road gets a row, because a default would be a guess.

column6: Walked, carted and patrolled end to end
The road they came in by and have ridden four times
They came UP it, so they know it is there and where it goes out of the hundred. They have not been back down it
Ridden by Wat and by Dave
Taken by cart twice
The eight miles of field track through Fenn's yard, walked and carted
Toller named it: three days east out of Ludbury to Wraye. Never travelled

*** THEY HAVE NEVER ASKED WHERE SIR AYMER'S CLIP GOES. *** It goes to Ludbury and it does not pass their town, which is most of why nobody in Wethersby could say where the staple went. One question to Ottir or Cuddy would open it

Durnhak described it down the shaft: round the crag's north shoulder, east then north along the foot of the scree, an hour's walk from the cave mouth. A bearing and a time, from a man with no reason to lie and no way to draw it
Coll's crew graded it and the party has walked it every expedition since day 20
Half an hour of unmade outcrop above the basecamp, walked eleven times

*** NOT WALKED, NOT SCOUTED, NOT CONFIRMED CART-PASSABLE. *** All the party has is that Durnhak's people get iron OFF the crag by their own route and that the watercourse mouth is round the north foot. That is a bearing and a claim, not a road

*** WALKED TO AND STOOD IN, day 98. *** Two miles north-east of the basecamp round the crag's north foot, found late in the afternoon off Durnhak's spoken bearing, which was exactly right. The vague ring at 1,500 ft comes off; the place is where he said it was

WALKED, day 98, out and back, leading three horses. NOT a trail and still not one -- but it is now ground the party has crossed rather than a line drawn on one sentence, and a led horse got round it, which is the cheapest test there was of whether a cart can follow
Ridden to and through, day 98. Three riders came off the waste and struck the road's last mile at about sunset
The last mile of the north road, ridden day 98 -- and it frays out to nothing, which nobody had ever gone north to see
Ridden end to end, day 98, by Dave, Yrtone and Hask. The whole point of the ride was to find out whether it would take a cart

*** NOT CART GROUND, AND THE PARTY PAID A DAY TO LEARN IT. *** Ridden on day 98 in the last of the light and it looked like firm open waste from the saddle. Under a loaded cart the crust breaks and the wheels cut in, and where it is not soft it is old frost-heave with stone under the turf. ~3 HOURS A MILE with a mule and two men at its head, and taking 232 lb off the load barely changed it -- THE GROUND IS THE PROBLEM, NOT THE WEIGHT. *** 3.7 miles of it on the loop route. THE GOAT LINE ROUND THE NORTH FOOT IS TWO MILES and walkable in an hour and twenty. *** THE RULE THE PARTY NOW OWNS: iron comes off this crag on shoulders and horses, not on wheels -- which is exactly how Durnhak has always moved it, with ten people and no cart at all.

Darrow named it plainly, asked directly what roads leave Ludbury: a direct road to Draycot, not through Wethersby at all -- about a hundred miles, four days by cart. This is the road Sir Aymer's own clip has travelled these two summers (district.md), which is WHY Wethersby was never told where his wool went. The party has always known THAT it goes to Ludbury; this is the first time anyone has been told HOW.
